doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Trio, swing and the piano players
title: The drumless trio and the John Wilson review of Bucky and John
summary: He explains why he returned to a drumless trio after Tony Tedesco's years, and reads a 1985 John Wilson review. Rowe asks about dropping a beat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah well it’s a — that’s — everything involved in the drumless trio, which we did — actually I think when I first talked to you we had drums in the group or were just starting to have more drums. Tony Tedesco played with us for years and it was really a monetary decision to go back to the drumless group because we were going to Europe and I said well we can’t afford this but I can do it with a drumless group because it gives me another harmonic instrument, the piano. So piano, guitar and bass. And I’m used to working in that format. I started out like that and that’s how I remember hearing my father’s group. So there’s something about that group that everybody’s got to be involved. Nobody can sort of sit back and say, “I just played my chorus” you know, “take it.” Everybody’s got to keep the motion moving. You know. And that’s what’s exciting about that. I love that sound — you know the rhythm guitar and coming up with figures that work with the piano and those kind of shout choruses and things like that. That’s one of the things. We have it in here. Speaking of — there’s a thing — it’s what Bucky and I, it’s based on that too — no this is John Wilson in December of ’85 when he says, “They come together on common ground at fast tempos when the hard-driving chorded attack that Bucky Pizzarelli has always used in these situations is picked up by his son, intensifying the rhythmic effect and enabling them to suggest a big band in full flight. The tiller-dillers or Benny Goodman’s band or the trumpet shakes of Count Basie’s.” That’s a great thing. It’s one of the first reviews that Bucky and I got and I keep it in my office.

Yes. And when you do that thing of the other guys drop out and it was uptempo and you’re doing this [scats] and I remember thinking, “Wow, is he going to make it?” First of all it just physically seems like a thing — I wonder if you’ve ever been doing that and you like drop a beat or add a beat?

There’s been definitely times when something goes wrong and I’ll even say it, you know, but the guys know where I am and they’ll get back and at the end — another thing like when I turn around and I’ll say, “I owe you a beat” or “I owe you a measure.” So there are those moments. Not as much as they used to be but there are those things. I’m not as, you know, who was it, you know the bands they can find ways to slide around the time
and they always land on their feet. And you know sometimes I like when that happens but if it keeps going, you know I drop my pick.
